description: Small team from Rzeszów, Poland. We build web apps on NASA Earth observation data: interactive maps, charts and clear stories around them. On board: frontend and backend developers, UX, plus video and pitch storytelling. We care about a working demo, a clear message and honest use of NASA data.
summary:
When It Burns is a web app that turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections into one consistent fire-activity calendar for any land area. Raw hotspot counts from MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) can't be compared directly: VIIRS has smaller pixels and sees smaller fires, so adding the counts creates a false jump in 2012. We fix this by counting 1 km grid cells with fire per day instead of single detections, then calibrating each sensor to the Suomi NPP VIIRS scale, month by month, over the years both sensors observed. Each calibrated value comes with an uncertainty range.

Users pick a ready-made region or draw their own. They get a calendar heatmap, the typical fire season and its critical weeks, an anomaly rating for any month, a statistically tested long-term trend, a map of detections and fire events, and CSV downloads. An experimental outlook, driven by a small neural network we trained ourselves on FIRMS data alone, estimates activity for the current month and the next two. This helps land managers, researchers and journalists answer two questions: when does this place usually burn, and is this month unusual?
details:
WHAT IT DOES
When It Burns builds a consistent, multi-year calendar of fire activity for any land area from NASA satellite hotspot detections. For a region the user picks or draws (up to 300,000 km²), it shows:

- Calendar heatmap: fire activity for every month or week since November 2000, with a switch between harmonized values and raw detection counts.
- Month detail: activity, long-term median, percentile, rank among years, days with fire, fire radiative power and per-sensor counts.
- Anomaly class: whether a month is below normal, normal, elevated or extreme, compared with that area's own history.
- Seasonality: the typical activity for each month or week across all years, the critical fire periods, and a running total showing how this year compares with the record so far.
- Long-term trend: a Mann–Kendall test with Theil–Sen slope on three series (harmonized, raw, MODIS alone), plus the trend of each calendar month.
- Map and fire events: individual detections shown as points or grid cells, coloured by power, date, sensor or day/night, with nearby detections grouped into fire events.
- Area comparison, and an overview of where the current month is unusual across ready-made areas.
- Experimental outlook: expected activity for the current month and the next two, shown only where it passed a backtest.
- CSV downloads of the calendar, the seasonality and the detections, a table view of every chart, and shareable links to any analysis.

Ready-made areas cover 230 countries and territories, the 16 Polish voivodeships, Biebrza National Park and six regions with well-known fires. Users can also draw a rectangle, circle, polygon or freehand shape, set the period, and filter by sensor, confidence, day or night, and vegetation fires only.

HOW IT WORKS (HARMONIZATION)
MODIS and VIIRS can't be compared directly. VIIRS pixels are 375 m instead of 1 km, so one fire produces several times more detections, and VIIRS also sees smaller, cooler fires. Our method:

1. Detections are put on a 0.01° grid (about 1 km, the size of a MODIS pixel). Each grid cell counts once per day. This "fire cell-day" removes most of the pixel-size difference.
2. Each calendar month is carried by one sensor, preferring Suomi NPP, then NOAA-20/21, then MODIS.
3. Every other sensor is calibrated onto the Suomi NPP scale with a separate factor for each calendar month, fitted over the years both sensors observed. Where a sensor saw too little fire for a monthly factor, one all-year factor is used. The spread between years gives an uncertainty range.
4. Days no satellite observed are treated as missing data, not as zero fire, and partial months are compared only with the same days in other years.
5. Built-in checks: a "2012 step test" measures whether the false jump is removed, reduced or still present for the chosen area, and the harmonized trend is cross-checked against the MODIS-only trend, which needs no harmonization. The app reports the result either way.

OUR OWN NEURAL NETWORK (EXPERIMENTAL OUTLOOK)
We trained a small feed-forward neural network (699 parameters) ourselves, offline with PyTorch, on FIRMS detections only. It has no pretrained weights and is not a language model. It uses the last twelve months of activity, the first days of the current month and the month's place in the season. A linear model and a damped-persistence rule are trained alongside it. For each country and each month ahead, a method is used only if it beat simple baselines on years it had never seen (2018–2025); otherwise no outlook is shown. The outlook describes the whole area's monthly activity. It does not say where or when a fire will start and is not a fire danger rating.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Fire managers, researchers, journalists and local authorities can see when an area usually burns, plan around critical weeks, and spot unusual months or long-term changes without having to understand sensor differences. Each area is compared with its own history, so a small national park and a large region can be compared fairly. Every number is calculated from NASA data with documented, deterministic rules, so the same question always gets the same answer.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES
- Frontend: SvelteKit (Svelte 5, TypeScript), Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL with Terra Draw, Apache ECharts, Turf.js, Paraglide (English and Polish).
- Backend: Node.js, Hono, Zod with an OpenAPI contract, DuckDB with its spatial extension over a Parquet dataset built from FIRMS CSV files.
- Outlook model: PyTorch, trained on FIRMS data only.
- Testing with Vitest, deployed with Docker.
- Claude Code (AI coding assistant) helped plan and write code, under the team's direction and review.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
Instead of hiding the difference between sensors, the app shows it. Users can switch to raw counts to see the 2012 jump, and harmonized values that came from MODIS are hatched and shown with an uncertainty range. The summaries are plain sentences built from templates filled with the calculated numbers, so no text is generated by a model. The app also says openly what it cannot do: a hotspot is not a fire, and small areas and quiet months get no forecast.
